title: Chapter VI

teacherSummary.text: Charlotte argues Jane should show more affection to secure Bingley, since 'happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.' Darcy begins to admire Elizabeth's 'fine eyes,' and Miss Bingley teases him about it.

vocabulary.context: “He is indeed—but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot wonder at his complaisance; for who would object to such a partner?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “complaisance”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Your friend performs delightfully;” he continued after a pause, on seeing Bingley join the group;—“and I doubt not that you are an adept in the science yourself, Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “perform”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly") + form (Latin forma, "shape"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To hide or withdraw from observation
vocabulary.context: If a woman conceals her affection with the same skill from the object of it, she may lose the opportunity of fixing him; and it will then be but poor consolation to believe the world equally in the dark.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conceal”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Darcy, “There is a fine old saying, which everybody here is of course familiar with—‘Keep your breath to cool your porridge,’—and I shall keep mine to swell my song.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “porridge”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: If I can perceive her regard for him, he must be a simpleton indeed not to discover it too.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “simpleton”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The union of man and woman as husband and wife
vocabulary.context: A lady’s imagination is very rapid; it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony in a moment.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “matrimony”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Supported on both sides by other charges
vocabulary.context: Her resistance had not injured her with the gentleman, and he was thinking of her with some complacency, when thus accosted by Miss Bingley—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “accosted”: ac- (Latin ad, "to") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Having the power or quality of exciting resentment
vocabulary.context: On his approaching them soon afterwards, though without seeming to have any intention of speaking, Miss Lucas defied her friend to mention such a subject to him, which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she turned to him and said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “provoking”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + vok (Latin vocare, "to call") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To make gross, thick, or large
vocabulary.context: Darcy stood near them in silent indignation at such a mode of passing the evening, to the exclusion of all conversation, and was too much engrossed by his own thoughts to perceive that Sir William Lucas was his neighbour, till Sir William thus began.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “engross”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To keep the mind in a state of contemplation
vocabulary.context: I have been meditating on the very great pleasure which a pair of fine eyes in the face of a pretty woman can bestow.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “meditate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Women could not propose; they had to signal interest within strict propriety.

significance: Charlotte's pragmatic view of marriage foreshadows her own choice later; Darcy's interest is the novel's first reversal.
discussionQuestions: Do you agree with Charlotte that happiness in marriage is a matter of chance?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VI,” how does Austen show strategy in courtship? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VI, how does Austen develop the idea of strategy in courtship? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VI develops the idea of strategy in courtship. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of strategy in courtship. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VI suggests about strategy in courtship. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter VI to complicate the reader's understanding of strategy in courtship. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of strategy in courtship responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of strategy in courtship follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VI and its treatment of strategy in courtship. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VI as evidence for a larger claim about strategy in courtship in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of strategy in courtship. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: On his approaching them soon afterwards, though without seeming to have any intention of speaking, Miss Lucas defied her friend to mention such a subject to him, which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she turned to him and said—

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Do you agree with Charlotte that happiness in marriage is a matter of chance? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are complaisance, performs, conceals, porridge, simpleton. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““He is indeed—but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot wonder at his complaisance; for who would object to such a partner?”” Webster's says: Disposition to please or oblige. Now the word history: “complaisance”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “perform”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly") + form (Latin forma, "shape"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “conceal”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Women could not propose; they had to signal interest within strict propriety. Why does this chapter matter? Charlotte's pragmatic view of marriage foreshadows her own choice later; Darcy's interest is the novel's first reversal. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to strategy in courtship.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
